articles.text: On Tuesday October 26, a Food and Drug Administration Advisory Committee met to discuss the emergency approval of BioNTech and Pfizer’s COVID- 19 vaccine for children 5-11 years old. The committee recommended that the FDA approve the vaccine for the age group. Formal FDA approval would mean that Piedmont students ages 5-11 would need to show proof of vaccination within eight weeks to attend school. The FDA is not required to follow the advice of its committee, but typically does. A final decision by the FDA on whether or not to allow emergency approval for children 5-11 is expected within a week. In its meeting on September 22, the Piedmont School Board mandated COVID-19 vaccination for all eligible students as a requirement for attending classes. Currently, students age 12 and up must provide proof of vaccination by Wednesday, November 17th. If the FDA approves the new age group, PUSD’s policy requires parents to provide the district with proof of vaccination within eight weeks, with the only caveat being a medical exemption. (Full vaccination is achieved two weeks after the second dose). Dr. George Rutherford, a UCSF epidemiologist and infectious disease expert, recommends waiting at least four weeks between the first and second shots. “I would try to stretch out the time between the first and second doses a little longer than three weeks; I would try four. The farther you can stretch it out the greater will be the protection that is provided. That is one of the reasons we are having problems with waning immunities because it was a three-week gap initially,” Rutherford explained. On Friday October 22 the FDA said that Pfizer’s case study of 2,268 elementary age students produced an efficacy rate of 90.7% against symptomatic infection seven days after their second shot. This efficacy results from a smaller dose than that given to people 12 and up receive, 10 micrograms instead of 30 micrograms. The most common side effects for this group occurred after the second dose and included pain at the injection site, fatigue, and headache. The FDA says no serious adverse events associated with the vaccine occurred in the study. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department will receive $100,000 from the California Citizens Option for Public Safety (COPS) grant. The City Council formally accepted the grant at its meeting on October 18. The state budget has included allocations to cities for its COPS program since 1997. The funding is allocated for services to ensure public safety at the local level, and must be used for frontline municipal police services and should not supplant existing funding. The funds must be spent or encumbered by June 30, 2022. The Police Depar tment received $100,000 from the COPS grant in fiscal year 2021- 22; in addition, $531,000 is being carried forward from prior years resulting in total available funds of $631,000. There are no matching requirements for the grant, and no direct impact on city resources. The funding will be used as follows: $320,000 toward public safety camera program and implementation; $20,000 toward social media consulting and web page support; $35,000 in overtime for community events, special patrol and other staff support; $220,000 toward facility updates, including updates to the briefing room; and $25,000 in National Incident-Based Reporting System (NIBRS) staff training. NIBRS is implemented to improve the overall quality of crime data collected by law enforcement. articles.text: The City of Piedmont has requested a second extension of the Measure A-1 application deadline. City Council made the request, which will be reviewed by the Alameda County Board of Supervisors. If granted, the city would have until December 31, 2023 to produce a project application that describes how it will use its $2.2 million allocation in county funds to develop affordable housing programs. In presenting the agenda item to the city council at an October 18 meeting, City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that the efforts of city staff, the Planning Commission, the city’s ad-hoc Measure A-1 subcommittee, and residents led to the recommendation for another extension of the county’s deadline. The city earlier received an extension of the deadline from December 31, 2021 to December 2022. “As we [discussed] for more than a year with how to best approach our 6th cycle housing element update, one that is so substantially different than anything we’ve been asked to tackle in the past, we continue to learn and wrap our heads around this process,” Lillevand said. She added that the recommendation to request an extension “makes for the most efficient and effective use of the city’s time and resources.” On September 13, the Planning Commission determined that the development of a multifamily affordable housing project on cityowned land would have a greater chance of attracting a developer, but that related zoning code revisions and CEQA-reviews would not be completed within the constraints of the current deadline the county set for applications. Piedmont’s application for the use of Measure A-1 funds is currently set at December 31, 2022, and, according to an accompanying staff report, a one-year extension would “align Measure A-1 efforts with [the city’s] Housing Element update timeline.” While the city council members present were in favor of an extension, concerns with how to approach the deadline extension were expressed. “This is absolutely the right approach, it’s clear that we’ve demonstrated that we’ve spent a lot of time thinking about A-1,” said council member Jen Cavenaugh, but added, “I’m not sure we’ve made the case in our argument, and why one more year isn’t sufficient.” Conna McCarthy questioned the probability of a second extension approval. Planning Director Kevin Jackson responded “that there was no indication it’s a slam-dunk, but that [the city] has a good case.” The city considered Measure A-1 funds as a potential source of funding for new incentives for constructions of accessory dwelling units (ADUs) that are rent-restricted for low and verylow income residents. However, residents and city staff have expressed interest in exploring other possibilities. “I’m very pleased that staff has embraced the notion of pivoting away from an ADU-centric philosophy of increasing our housing. We’re really looking to explore more creative opportunities,” Mayor Teddy Gray King said. “We are experiencing a time in Piedmont where we truly have an organized, vocal, passionate group of Piedmonters who want to explore those opportunities.” Lillevand noted that, upon city council’s approval of the extension, the city would “dive into preliminary site assessment of city-owned properties.” Residents speak up Deborah Leland, Chair of the Budget Advisory & Financial Planning Committee, offered her support of the extension, and added that the city government should utilize the acreage it owns in Piedmont when exploring lots for fair housing. “I’m in support of moving away from using Measure A-1 for ADU (accessory dwelling unit) financing, and instead seeking the time necessary to pursue using those funds for affordable rental housing,” she said. “The city... is by far the largest landowner in Piedmont, owning 64 acres of land. Taking a close look at cityowned property is both reasonable and necessary,” she said. articles.text: In responding to a resident requesting clarification about the use of “premium bonds” for the construction of a community pool under the provisions of Measure UU, City Clerk John Tulloch explained: “I am writing in response to your inquiry pertaining to the use of Premium Bonds for Measure UU. The City forwarded your request for legal analysis to the City’s Bond Counsel. They provided a response that I am sharing and paraphrasing below. “The legal authority for the City to issue General Obligation Bonds, whether at par, premium or discount, is embedded in the California Constitution and codes, the City Charter, and related ordinances and resolutions of the City Council. For example, California Government Code Section 53508.7 provides, ‘The bonds shall be sold at a public or private sale and at a price at, above, or below par, as the legislative body determines.’ “As approved by the voters in Measure UU, the City has the legal authority to sell bonds in a principal (par) amount that does not exceed $19.5 million and at an interest rate that does not exceed 12%. Accordingly, the City may sell the bonds in a principal amount of up to $19.5 million. In addition, subject to the 12% interest rate cap, the City may sell the bonds at a price above par, thereby generating additional proceeds in the form of original issue premium. “At the time Measure UU was being considered by City Council, given then-current interest rates, it was anticipated that the sale of bonds in the principal amount of $19.5 million may yield more than $23.0 million in proceeds, with the difference being the payment of an original issue premium by investors in the City’s bonds. The amount of original issue premium paid by investors will depend upon market conditions at the time of sale of the bonds. The bonds will be priced so the median rate paid by the taxpayers is consistent with the Tax Rate Statement included in the Measure UU documents.”
articles.title: Defining premium bonds for pool project

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Western Neighborhoods Project The Museum at The Cliff held an opening party on October 23. Spearheaded by the Western Neighborhoods Project, the pop-up aims to promote the rich history of the building and Sutro Baths as the National Park Service searches for a new, long-term tenant. A temporary pop-up museum has opened at the former Cliff House gift shop, and now is open to the general public until midThe Cliff House restaurant, housed in a historic building perched above the cliffs just north of Ocean Beach in San Francisco, closed last year due to leasing issues with the National Park Service (NPS) and dining closures brought on by the pandemic. The Cliff House’s main draw since 1863 had been the magnificent Pacific Ocean views. Though the NPS has said it is “committed to maintaining the iconic building,” the long-term future of the space is unknown. On February 2, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors passed a resolution urging the NPS to find an immediate vendor for the space while it searches for a long-term tenant. On Saturday, October 23, the Western Neighborhoods Project, a nonprofit based in the Inner Richmond district and dedicated to preserving San Francisco history, opened a temporary museum open to the public inside the former Cliff House gift shop. The pop-up museum is in partnership with Art Conservation and The Great Highway gallery, with support from the Golden Gate National Recreation Area’s Park Archives and Records Center. Some artifacts likely to be on display are swimsuits from the Sutro Baths, an 1890’s stool belonging to Adolph Sutro, a luncheon menu from President Teddy Roosevelt’s visit to the restaurant in 1903, and many more. “I’m so proud of [the] efforts to preserve many of the historical artifacts that create this wonderful museum while the National Park Service searches for a new vendor for the Cliff House,” said San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, who serves District 1, where Cliff House is located. The museum will be open to the public from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. through April 2022.

Though the NPS has said it is “committed to maintaining the iconic building,” the long-term future of the space is unknown. On February 2, the San Francisco Board of Supervisors passed a resolution urging the NPS to find an immediate vendor for the space while it searches for a long-term tenant. On Saturday, October 23, the Western Neighborhoods Project, a nonprofit based in the Inner Richmond district and dedicated to preserving San Francisco history, opened a temporary museum open to the public inside the former Cliff House gift shop. The pop-up museum is in partnership with Art Conservation and The Great Highway gallery, with support from the Golden Gate National Recreation Area’s Park Archives and Records Center. Some artifacts likely to be on display are swimsuits from the Sutro Baths, an 1890’s stool belonging to Adolph Sutro, a luncheon menu from President Teddy Roosevelt’s visit to the restaurant in 1903, and many more. “I’m so proud of [the] efforts to preserve many of the historical artifacts that create this wonderful museum while the National Park Service searches for a new vendor for the Cliff House,” said San Francisco Supervisor Connie Chan, who serves District 1, where Cliff House is located. The museum will be open to the public from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. through April 2022. articles.text: School Board to discuss H1 Bond budget at tonight’s meeting Members of the Piedmont School Board will receive an update at tonight’s meeting on both the cost and timeline overruns of the STEAM classroom building and the theater building still in construction. The meeting, October 27, will be at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall. Voters approved up to $66 million for school construction based upon the H1 public Bond. It was intended to cover all costs for the two buildings, and have some money for additional projects. According to the school district, unforeseen and added costs “contributed roughly $6.5 million to bond program costs.” The increased cost now puts the total for the two buildings at $70.3 million. Financing options will be discussed during the meeting. The school board’s background document includes the following: • California’s Division of State Architect (DSA) mandating changes which added significant quantities of structural steel and concrete. • Required overtime labor to ensure STEAM completion for the start of the 2020-21 school year. (Overtime was later discontinued when Covid canceled in-person classes, and urgency to reopen.) • Discovery and replacement of deteriorating underground utilities for all existing high school buildings and discovery and repair of a dangerous underground void beneath the PHS breezeway. • Pandemic-related costs including a full-time health and safety officer at the STEAM and theater construction sites, and additional shifts for fewer workers and Covid spacing. • Relocation and upgrade of the District internet server room, including new servers, switches, and battery storage. • Necessary shoring for the theater foundation and an unexpected new concrete driveway. • Costs of theatrical lighting fixtures and controls that were discontinued due to Covid-19. “The District worked with Overaa [Construction, the general contractor] and its subcontractors to offset more than half of these costs without compromising the life cycle of the buildings or educational programs... The District [also] deferred certain features including: solar panels; furnishings, fixtures, and equipment for the black box theater; and other items that can be added later when additional funding becomes available,” wrote School Superintendent Randy Booker. “Value engineering” and deferment of features offset some of the added costs, but there is still a shortfall of up to $2.9 million. That amount does not include deferred items, including the theater’s orchestral shell, acoustical panels, and solar panels. Last year, Piedmont students began a fundraising campaign to pay for the missing solar panels on the classroom building. The board will discuss ways to pay for the overages at tomorrow’s meeting. A background document lists a $4-6 million state bond they could receive but which is contingent upon a state election item. “The timing of receipt is uncertain because it depends on the approval of a statewide school construction bond measure,” Booker stated. The full document can be viewed at Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/Meetings/Attachment.aspx?S=36030373&AID=1 79483&MID=9077. Options to cover costs until possibly receiving money from the state will be discussed at future meetings. “The options include a no-interest loan of up to $1.8 million from the Piedmont Education Foundation, and financing from Overaa for the full amount of anticipated State funds for a term of up to three years,” Booker stated in the document. Members of the community can attend the meeting in person at 7:00 p.m., or view on Zoom. To register, click on https://us06web. zoom.us/j/86434103152. Piedmont City Hall is located at 120 Vista Avenue.

articles.text: The Question: “My child gets A’s on homework and quizzes, and is confident she knows the material, but then does poorly on tests. Is she just a bad test taker?” The Answer: Possibly to a degree, but it is likely that the problem has more to do with preparing for tests than taking them. Good Test Takers There are some skills that do make some kids better at taking tests than others: rote memory, attention and strategic test taking. Attention and memory are skills that can be developed, but as cognitive skills they are harder to improve. Strategic test taking is something that most students can improve right away. Strategic Test Takers Strategic test taking means thinking not just about the information that is being asked, but thinking about how the test is structured, the way in which the questions are being asked, what might the “trick” be for a question, and what the teacher thinks is important. Preparation is more important than test taking In reality, doing well on a test is far more about preparation than test taking. So, what can a student do to prepare for a test? • Know the test • Study • Develop understanding • Maintain your knowledge Know the test Too many students don’t take the time to find out what will be Preparation is the key to positive test results. covered, what type of questions will be asked, or how best to prepare. These are things that every student should find out before preparing for the test, so that they know what and how to study. • What is covered • Test Structure • How Best to Prepare Study - More than just doing homework A lot of students think “studying” means doing all of their assignments and review sheets. They do not realize that studying involves independently figuring out what material they need to know and taking the time to learn it, even if that has not been assigned or outlined. Understand completely There are many stages of understanding and each stage builds upon the last. Understanding can be broken into the following 5 levels: recognizing, remembering, repeating, understanding and utilizing. 1. Recognizing – Follow when the teacher does it. 2. Remembering – Remember what the teacher did. 3. Repeating – Do what the teacher does. 4. Understanding – Know why each step in a process is taken. 5. Utilizing – Use the process to solve types of problems.

Seeing progress is important. Taking practice tests that give an actual score can invigorate that competitive spirit. While there are many great online resources for practice tests and studying, it is important to familiarize yourself with the format of the test which will be on paper. Most students have not taken a test that lasts over an hour, so get ready for the SAT – a three-hour test with one 10-minute break and one five-minute break. Make sure to “practice like you play,” by sitting down and simulating the long haul. If your test is scheduled for 9:00 a.m. on a Saturday, taking a practice test at the same time and day will add routine and comfort to the actual morning of the test. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: After a one year hiatus, ghouls and goblins will be anxious to return to the Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade on Saturday, October 30, starting at 11:00 a.m. (shown here in 2010). The Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade, a treasured public event since 1986, returns this year after last year’s hiatus due COVID-19 and related restrictions. The 34th annual Piedmont Avenue Halloween Parade will take place this Saturday, October 30, starting at 11:00 a.m. at the corner of Montell Street and Piedmont Avenue. The event is family-friendly and geared to youth, organized by the Piedmont Avenue Merchants Association. Come in costume and stop by the shops along Piedmont Avenue for trick-or-treating opportunities. The annual pet costume contest, held concurrently with the parade, is at 12:30 p.m. at Pet Food Express. The Piedmont Avenue Elementary School PTA is sponsoring events on the school playground from 11:30 a.m. to 1:30 p.m., including “trunk-or-treating.” Parents must accompany their children to this free event. The event will be held outdoors, but masks and face-coverings are encouraged per county guidelines.

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek is celebrating Halloween with a green twist. Visit the gardens on Saturday, October 30, for “Aloe-ween.” Dress up in costume for this family-friendly event, running from 10 a.m. until 1 p.m. There will be a pumpkin scavenger hunt for kids - find all the hidden pumpkins in the gardens and win a prize. A food drive supporting the Food Bank of Contra Costa will be accepting non-perishable food and canned items for Thanksgiving meals. A youth-focused costume contest will be conducted – costumed pets are welcome, too. Kids will enjoy a visit from staff at Papaya Pythons. Herpetologists will teach audience members about reptiles and amphibians and how important they are to their respective ecosystems. There will also be a visit from the garden’s resident “Cactus Lady.” RSVP is required for this event. Dogs on leash are welcome. To RSVP, visit https:// www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/ event/aloe-ween-at-the-garden-2021/.

articles.text: The Piedmont High cross country program traveled to Cordova High School near Sacramento on Saturday, October 23 for the Postal Nationals, a 3,200- meter event. Schools throughout the country upload their two-mile times into a database. The course at Cordova High is 3200 meters, comparable to a 2-mile race in track. Piedmont’s boys’ team finished 6th among 52 California schools, and the girls placed 8th in a field of 27 teams. “The two-mile event is a nationwide competition with teams posting their best 3,200- meter times for comparison across the country. We were lucky to be invited to a live rendition of the full race experience at Cordova High. It was a thrill to watch 3,200 racing, it felt much shorter than our traditional 3-mile events for cross country,” said coach Jeanine Holmlund. The Highlanders also ran a 5K event at Oyster Bay in San Leandro two days earlier, Wednesday, October 21. Piedmont’s boys’ team was fastest among 10 schools, and the girls finished 3rd among nine teams. Jack Stein led the way for Piedmont in both events, finishing the Postal Nationals with a time of 9:54.27 to finish fifth in a crowded field of 123 runners. He won the League Center Meet on Thursday with a time of 16:25.99. As for the girls, sophomore breakout performer Josephine Oesterer also led both events, clocking an 11:44.23 at Postal Nationals to finish 14th of 99 runners at Cordova while winning the WACC 5K at Oyster Bay with a time of 19:27.81 against 66 runners. Postal Nationals recap On an overcast Saturday in Rancho Cordova, Piedmont’s boys’ team placed sixth, with Jesuit, Trabuco Hills, McClatchy, Dana Hills, and Sacred Heart as the top five. Stein led Piedmont with an overall fifth-place finish in a field of 153 runners, followed closely by super sophomore Xander Schulte-Sasse in ninth with a time of 10:03.02. Junior Christian Taylor crossed the finish line five seconds later for 11th place, and Parker Long placed 14th in 10:16.69. Piedmont’s boys’ team continued to display strong pack running (5th, 9th, 11th, 14th). The girls’ team placed 8th out of 27 schools, led by Josie Oesterer with a 14th place overall finish in 11:44.23. Sophomore Jamie Schwarz was 19th in 11:52.33 in a field of 99. Mara Lovric placed 32nd in 12:38.07, Violet Lemley finished 49th in 13:17.57, and senior Molly McWeeny came in 59th, 13:34.03. articles.text: Piedmont’s Homecoming football game with Bishop O’Dowd was exciting for the first half on Friday night, October 22, when the Highlanders led O’Dowd 8-7. The second half, however, was a completely different story, and the Dragons rebounded to win 31-8. Piedmont’s depleted varsity roster of 17 players did what it could, but the wear and tear on the starters – with most on the roster playing both offense and defense – began to show. Trailing O’Dowd by one touchdown heading into the last quarter, 14-8, the Dragons ran away for a 31-8 win. The halftime lead against O’Dowd – a perennial football powerhouse in Oakland – was the first in at least five years. “I’ll be looking at the film to see why we gave up the edge,” said coach Jerome Johnson. “On offense, we couldn’t get better field position. Once again, we had some mental mistakes, and it reflects on the score.” Piedmont defensive lineman Mason Kimball had a big day with one QB sack, three tackles for loss, and two forced fumbles. “Mason Kimball is our anchor and our rock. He is our inside rusher and he keeps pressure and pushes the pocket. He and Ethan Feldstein set the tone on the inside,” said Johnson. The defense fought valiantly to achieve eight tackles for loss, four sacks, two interceptions, two fumble recoveries, and three forced fumbles. Game Recap PHS opened the game with an onside kick attempt and forced a turnover on downs at their own 49 yard line by stopping BOD’s receiver short of a first down on a 4th down. After a Piedmont-punt, O’Dowd retained possession at the 50 and drove to Piedmont’s 25-yard line. Bailey Cain recorded a sack for a loss of six yards to force 3rd-and-15. Defensive back Ryan McConathy then knocked a pass down to make it fourth down. An incompletion on fourth down gave Piedmont possession again. The two sides traded possession once more to end the first quarter in a 0-0 deadlock. PHS opened the second quarter at its 19 yard line and began to move. A Dragon defensive back got his hand on the ball to force a fumble at the BOD 45-yard line. On its next play, a long pass over the top of the defense connected for a 55 yard touchdown pass and a 7-0 lead for O’Dowd. But Piedmont came firing back with wide receiver Defazio taking a 62-yard catch and run to the BOD six yard line. At the two-yard line, the offense called a designed stretch run for quarterback Adhi Bornstein. He was met by a swarm of defenders who knocked the ball loose at the twoyard line and a fumble recovery. On O’Dowd’s next possession, Ryan McConathy was able to strip the ball loose from the Dragon running back at the five yard line. The ball was scooped up at the goal line by O’Dowd, but Lucas Bernales and Battista Costa tackled him in the end zone for a safety, making the score 7-2. On a 4th down, Piedmont was unable to make a first down at O’Dowd’s 41-yard line, and the Dragons worked the ball to Piedmont’s 45/ They attempted another bomb down the sideline, but this time the ball was intercepted by Defazio in the end zone and returned to the 31. From there, PHS drove to the BOD 49, but was stopped on 4th-and-9 with 33 seconds left in the half. The Dragons tried two pass plays that ended in Piedmont’s favor. The first play resulted in Kimball blitzing the quarterback for an eight-yard loss, a fumble but recovery by the Dragons. On 2nd-and-18 with time expiring, the Dragons looked deep again, but Kimball made his second consecutive sack and forced fumble. This time, the ball was scooped up by Cain for a 35-yard touchdown run, and an 8-7 Piedmont lead at halftime. In the second half, PHS turned the ball over on an interception at the BOD 42. The Dragons turned it into a 22 yard touchdown carry and 14-8 lead with 10:47 left in the third quarter. articles.text: Piedmont’s volleyball team wrapped up its season on Thursday, October 21 at Binks Rawlings Gym with a nail-biting 3-2 loss to Berkeley, 22-25, 25-18, 25-12, 21-25, 16-14. “Even though we got the loss, it felt like a win,” said coach Leslie Blakely. “We got into a five-set match after they swept us 3-0 earlier in the season. We played really well and showed good energy and that fight that we have. I’m super proud of them.” The Highlanders honored the five seniors on the roster prior to Thursday’s game, including Ruby Shaffer, Sofia Croley, Ari Talwatte, Sophie Nevis, and Amelia Wire. “It was an emotional game. It could’ve gone better over the last couple of points, but it was a great game to end on. These girls are going to do so well, I can’t wait to see them lead,” said Shaffer, a captain on the team. Although the squad finished with a 3-12 record, the team fought valiantly in front of a roaring crowd to the finish. The squad has some talented underclassmen in important roles, including Bree DeYoung, Lila Town, Sadie Town, Eden Lorin, Tara Kothari, Izzy Grimmer, and Bauer Peterson. “It makes me so happy to see how much of an impact you can make as a senior. You can empower other players and make the team stronger as a community. Next year the girls are going to be so strong; they have already built that tight-knit connection. I’m really sad to leave and stop playing with my close friends, but it’s nice to end on this note,” said Talwatte. Volleyball will return to Binks Rawlings Gym in the spring a boys’ team, also coached by Blakely. Game Recap The Highlanders opened with a triumphant 25-22 win in the first game, but fell 25-18 in the second and 25-12 in the third. Piedmont won the fourth game 25-21, and forced an extra point in the fifth, but Berkeley closed it out with a narrow 16-14 victory in the fifth set. Berkeley’s new head coach is Alison West, the former coach at Piedmont who helped lead PHS to the North Coast Section playoffs. West’s final year in Piedmont was the last time the Highlanders reached the postseason. In the first game, Berkeley opened to a 5-1 lead, but Piedmont eventually powered ahead 9-8 with five straight points when trailing 8-4. While down 19-16, PHS’ Nevis smacked down two spikes along with an offensive error from BHS to tie 19-19. After back and forth scoring, PHS tied at 22-22 then gained three straight points to win due to offensive errors by the Jackets, 25-22 Piedmont. But the Highlanders couldn’t find similar fluidity in the second game, falling 25-18 after allowing seven straight points to open. Berkeley held Game Point at 24-13; PHS rallied five straight points to 24-18, but an offensive error was the end of it, 25-18. In the third, the two sides traded points until Berkeley held a 9-6 lead—then it was all Jackets, going on to score the next nine of 10 points to jump ahead 18-7. They closed out strong, 25-12. In the fourth set, Piedmont did well to limit rallies and jumped out to a 6-2 lead to start. Berkeley was able to tie at 13-13, but PHS gained five straight points to go ahead 18-13. DeYoung closed the game with a powerful spike into the Jackets’ midcourt, 25-21. In the fifth and final game, Piedmont opened with a 6-1 lead with help of two spikes by Shaffer and an ace by Wire. Two aces by Lila Town to make it 10-6, but Berkeley was able to eventually tie at 12-12 and gain match point at 14-12. A service error by Berkeley made it 14-13, while Nevis sent in an ace to tie it at 14-14. However, a pair of offensive errors helped Berkeley finish things with a win, 16-14. Final stats: Shaffer with eight kills and three aces; Wire had six kills and an ace; Nevis had six spikes and an ace; Talwatte had six spikes and an ace; DeYoung had five spikes; Sadie Town and her sister Lila each had two aces. Ruby Shaffer goes up for a spike. She had eight on the night. Senior Ari Talwatte had six kills and an ace.
articles.title: Volleyball ends season with 3-2 loss to Berkeley

articles.text: Belmont-based First Generation Swim Foundation has launched a scholarship program for free swim lessons for Bay Area kids who are the first in their family to learn how to swim. Families may complete the online application at www.firstswimmer.org/apply for English or www.firstswimmer.org/apply-inspanish for Spanish. Ten scholarships will be awarded to local children ages four to 16. With 20 percent of all drowning victims age 15 or younger, Zane Tanabe started a foundation to combat this danger. He noticed that many of the parents of his teammates on the swim and water polo teams didn’t know how to swim. “Swimming saves lives, and no one has taught first generation swimmers these skills. My hope is that this foundation will give them the chance to learn,” said Tanabe. First Generation Swim Foundation is a 501c3 nonprofit organization with the mission of preventing under-resourced Bay Area kids from drowning by giving free swim lessons to those who are the first in their family to learn to swim. Zane Tanabe, the founder of First Generation Swim Foundation, is a Belmont resident and sophomore at Sacred Heart Preparatory, where hs is a varsity swimmer and water polo player.

articles.text: An art exhibition entitled Suspended Matter will open at Berkeley Art Center on October 30. The exhibition will be on display through January 15, 2022. Suspended Matter features the work of artists Julia Goodman, Asma Kazmi, Laura Arminda Kingsley, and Jenifer K. Wofford, and is curated by Patricia Cariño Valdez. Through various mediums including sculpture, video, photography, and paintings, the artists consider connections between humanity and the domestic objects that shape our environments and surroundings. The name of the exhibition is a riff off the scientific definition of a “disruption in the environment,” such as erosion or flooding. “The works in Suspended Matter contemplate how we interact with others and our surroundings,” said Carino Valdez. “From the reconstitution of familiar fabrics into abstract shapes as seen in Goodman’s sculptures to a close examination of domestic objects that we interact within Kazmi’s work, the artists recognize the shifting interactions with our values, beliefs, and the everyday objects that we keep. The otherworldly sci-fi videos by Kingsley and Wofford’s depictions of solitude and isolation remind us of the constant revaluation of our existence and our resilience in relation to the past and present.” Berkeley Art Center is located at 1275 Walnut Street in North Berkeley. For more information call (510) 644-6893.

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory Theatre will reopen on November 12 with a live production of Wintertime by Charles Mee and directed by Les Waters. It will be performed until December 19. Berkeley Rep welcomes back Mee and Les Waters who have teamed up in the past to bring Fetes de la Nuit and Big Love to the stage. Wintertime is the story of a “gloriously eccentric family who arrive at their summer house in the winter woods for supposedly secret rendezvous—and soon bodies collide, doors slam, dishes fly, and everyone’s perfect plans go fantastically awry.” The cast stars James Carpenter as Frank, Sharon Lockwood as Hilda, and includes Carmen Berkeley as Ariel, Nora El Samahy as Mariam, and Sarah Nina Hayon as Jaqueline. Tickets are now on sale. Berkeley Rep requires all audience members to present a vaccination card with matching photo identification, and to be fully masked. All productions take place at Roda Theatre at 2015 Addison Street in Berkeley. Visit https://www.berkeleyrep. org/shows/wintertime/ to purchase tickets. Berkeley Repertory Theatre on Addison Street.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD), a Smithsonian affiliate, will present an exhibition in partnership with Contemporary Arts Museum of Houston entitled “Amoako Boafo: Soul of Black Folks.” The exhibition opened on October 20 and will be on display through February 27. It is the premier museum solo exhibition for Ghanian artist Amoako Boafo and includes more than 20 works created between 2018 and 2021. Curated by Larry Ossei-Mensah, it displays the artist’s paintings that show his calculated brushwork and finger-painted strokes. Boafo’s paintings are intimately connected to his experience as a Ghanaian artist living and working between Vienna, Austria, and Accra, Ghana. The text by American sociologist, civil rights activist, and author W.E.B Du Bois inspires the exhibition title which aims to be a study of “Black life behind the veil of race.” The Museum of the African Diaspora is located at 685 Mission Street in San Francisco. To learn more about the exhibition, visit https://www.moadsf. org/exhibition/amoako-boafosoul-of-black-folks/. articles.text: Jayden Lee (Leon Jones, right) and his mom, Crystal (Velina Brown) play a game in The Great Khan, now playing at San Francisco Playhouse on Post Street. San Francisco Playhouse will present The Great Khan on stage now through November 13. The show is written by Michael Gene Sullivan, the prolific writer of shows for the long-running San Francisco Mime Troupe. The Great Khan will be directed by Darryl Jones, and stars Velina Brown (Crystal), Leon Jones (Jayden) and Jamella Cross (Ant). The story follows protagonist Jayden, an African American teenage boy who saves a girl, Ant, from sexual assault. Following the incident, Jayden and his mother are forced to move to keep him safe from the boys who attacked Ant. Both Ant and Jayden try to figure out how to define themselves in a culture that insists on seeing them as forever dangerous. The Great Khan is in a rolling world premiere through the National New Play Network. Tickets are available with a seating chart with fixed social distancing. Masks will be required during the performance. Proof of vaccination against COVID-19 is required for all audience members. Visit www.sfplayhouse.org to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Cal Performances welcomes singer-songwriter Angelique Kidjo as the organization’s first season-long artist-in-residence. She will perform her unique take on the Talking Head’s 1980 album Remain in Light this Friday, October 29 at Zellerbach Hall. “One of the great pleasures this season is welcoming Angélique Kidjo, who hasn’t appeared here in nearly a decade, back to Berkeley as our first season-long artist-in-residence,” said Jeremy Geffen, Cal Performances’ artistic director. “Having been a presenter, collaborator and fan of her work for years, I know firsthand of her passion, conviction, and boundless curiosity. She brings inextinguishable energy to bear in both her performances and her community outreach work.” Kidjo is a four-time Grammy winner and was recently named one of Time Magazine’s “100 most influential people of 2021” for her work in the arts and as a cultural ambassador. The artist, who fled a dictatorship in her home country of Benin, draws from her personal experiences when creating music. Kidjo’s latest recording, Mother Nature, was released earlier this year and incorporates West African music, Afrobeat, Afro-pop, hip hop, and R&B. “Angélique draws from her personal experiences a deep sense Photo courtesy of Cultural Services of the French Embassy Angelique Kidjo of conviction as well as profound passion for exploring the breadth and depth of the human experience—qualities that make her the perfect partner for our season-long Illuminations programming,” said Geffen. “And most importantly, she comes to our campus hoping to learn as much as to share.” “By inviting her to meet with faculty and students, Cal Performances reinforces and supports the university’s values of cultivating and sustaining a diverse, equitable, informed, and inclusive and accessible community.” The concert begins at 8 p.m. Tickets range from $36 to $96. Half-price tickets are available for UC Berkeley students. Tickets are available through the Ticket Office at Zellerbach Hall, at (510) 642-9988, at calperformances. org, and at the door. Enluis Montes Olivar will serve as conductor for this special event. Members of the San Francisco Symphony will be joined by violinist Alexander Barantschik, vocalist Flor Amargo, and the Casa Circulo Cultural collective. articles.text: Oakland Ballet opens its season with Luna Mexicana, celebrating Dia de Los Muertos. Oakland Ballet will perform a special event entitled “Luna Mexicana” in honor of Dia de Los Muertos (Day of the Dead) on Friday and Saturday, November 5-6, at the Paramount Theatre. “Luna Mexicana” is one of the Bay Area’s most elaborate and inclusive events for the holiday celebrated and observed mostly in Mexico. It is a blend of exuberant and traditional dance, joyful music, vibrant costumes, flowers, candles, and food - orchestrated as a celebration of family and loved ones. Prior to the event, visit the Paramount Theatre lobby to view the ofrendas created by local artists. The dance performance will be 90 minutes with no intermission. Friday night’s performance is at 7:30 p.m., and the Saturday performance is a 2 p.m. matinee. Doors will open 60 minutes in advance. For tickets and more information, visit https://oaklandballet.org/performances-events/ luna-mexicana/.

articles.text: Notable twentieth century classical music theorist Heinrich Schenker and leading developer of bebop Charlie Parker both used core melody. Schenkerian analysis expresses the harmonic and melodic essence of a piece of music. While building a library of Parker phrases, I was listening to the head melody (the main thematic section) at seventy percent speed, to transcribe his performance on “Confirmation” and “Moose the Moochie.” I noticed he was playing the essential notes in each phrase with more dynamic accent. These “core melody” tones can be memorized as a melodic framework and elaborated differently each time you improvise. Now, in addition to an analysis of his melodic design, I could be cued by his louder notes. Use the link below to see and hear my use of Charlie Parker’s core melody concept and other attributes of his playing to create improvisations in his style: www.guitarimprov.com/ParkersCoreMelody.pdf Parker’s “dual melody” design is an imitation of two-voice counterpoint on one instrument. Play one or more notes of a melody in the high range of pitch, beginning a second melody with one or more notes in the low range, then alternate between the two ranges. In his “V” design, the melodic line goes up/down or down/up with a quick, ornate melodic figure at the peak or valley. You can read more in this excerpt from the Melodic Cells chapter of Guitar Improv: www. guitarimprov.com/zz-Charlie_ Parker_Design.pdf In his late teens, Parker practiced 12 hours daily, building his chops on his axe in a remote woodshed. He made this claim in a 1954 interview with Paul Desmond. Many people exaggerate in such claims, but judging by his playing, it seems true. Bandleader Jay McShann recalled that when their touring car ran over a chicken, Parker asked to go back and pick it up and cook it for dinner. From then on, his nickname was “Yardbird” (a.k.a. Bird). In 1939, Parker was looking for something new. In his words, “I was working over “Cherokee” and as I did, I found that by using the higher intervals of a chord as a melody line and backing them with appropriately related changes, I could play the thing I’d been hearing. I came alive.” He’s referring to the ninths, elevenths and thirteenths, which he featured the rest of his life. The high note in the first phrase of Duke Ellington’s “In a Sentimental Mood” is an eleventh. Jamming after hours at Monroe’s Uptown House and Minton’s Playhouse in Harlem in 1939-1941, Parker developed a new concept of melody and chord progression in his association with trumpeter Dizzy Gillespie and pianist Thelonius Monk. They took their contemporary Art Tatum’s reharmonization of chord progression into more dissonant territory. Jim Gleason is an author and guitar instructor. articles.text: Local artist Michael Stehr will present a new exhibit, The Other Side of the Fence: Considering Green and the Power of Color, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The exhibit is dedicated in loving memory of the artist’s mother, Bonnie Drewes Stehr, who recently died. Gallery hours are Saturdays and Sundays, from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. from November 13 to 21. A reception will be held on Friday evening, November 12. To attend the reception, RSVP to Michael at mstehrart@gmail.com. Red is hot, blue is cold, and yellow was known to make Van Gogh smile. While our reaction to color is affected greatly by personal preference, there is no denying that color has the ability to make one feel while eliciting a tangible reaction. In this exhibit Stehr explores the power of color by focusing on the impact of green. In 1140, stained glass at Notre Dame de Chartres showing Christ on the cross has the crucifix depicted in a green color, despite the fact that we know the cross was made of wood and was likely a shade of brown. Of course, green is associated with life ... rolling green hills in Spring, a lush forest, or a perfectly manicured baseball field ... all images that can elicit feelings of growth, vitality, and renewal. The cross depicted as green refers to the renewal that one’s soul can experience due to the sacrifice of Jesus on that cross. We encounter green in our daily lives in various shades. There is the brilliant green of a lawn encountered in morning light. There is the neutralized green of an oak tree that can almost appear warm under the light of early evening. Furthermore, the greens one perceives in a foreground change greatly viewing them at a distance. The exhibit will include 30 new paintings in which the color green has an important role in the impact of the painting. Stehr will address the chemistry of green as he discusses how he mixes green to achieve the various effects. Also being exhibited are 45 paintings from previous exhibitions. articles.text: Chris Evans as Captain America. Review by Chris Honore’ Who are these pulp fiction superheroes and why do they resonate with our children? Whatever the answer, Hollywood is in love with the comic book genre, especially with tales from the archives of DC and Marvel Comics. Summer blockbusters recently have been defined by the superhero: Thor, X-Men: First Class, Green Lantern, and not to forget Transformers. Plus Harry Potter, a superhero to be sure. Ask Voldermort. Now comes Marvel’s Captain America: The First Avenger. Consider the setup: a 90-pound weakling, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans ala CGI), is desperate to join the army and fight the Nazis (“I hate bullies” he says), but can’t pass the physical. He is recruited and transformed (using Super-Soldier serum) into a totally ripped G.I. Joe, aka Captain America, replete with shield, mask and tights. What 90-pound kid wouldn’t love to suddenly have the washboard abs of Captain America, an all-American hero who goes off to fight not just the Nazis, but a ratcheted up version of the evil doers, an outfit called Hydra, led by Red Skull (Hugo Weaving), who also possess some serious weaponry. This first Captain America is an origin film (beginning in 1942), and act one is devoted to how Rogers morphs into his present incarnation. It’s all nicely done, albeit with holes in the logic, requiring serious suspension of disbelief as well as a huge assist by CGI. But then, that’s what defines these wonderfully imagined movies. “No way” some literalists might say. Response: a chorus of kids saying, “Yes, way!” Captain America fights for truth, justice, and VE-day, which means serious combat with the Hydra. Sequel to follow. Captain America: The First Avenger. Directed by Joe Johnston. Starring Chris Evans, Haley Atwell, Tommy Lee Jones, Hugo Weaving and Stanley Tucci. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13.

articles.text: Friends With Benefits is not your grandfather’s movie. In the 1939 film, Gone With the Wind, Vivien Leigh asks Clark Gable, “What shall I do? Where shall I go?” He turns and says, “Frankly my dear, I don’t give a damn.” That singular word, “damn,” evoked gasps from audiences and represented a sea change in movies. And it was the beginning of a gradual loosening of film censorship regarding not only language but the interaction between men and women (physical and verbal). Until the late 1950s, Ozzie and Harriet slept in separate beds and everyone had a robe handy. Decorum and restraint ruled. But that was then and this is now, and romantic comedies such as Friends With Benefits definitely represent another sea change in terms of language and physical contact. True, “FWB” has outstanding portrayals by Mila Kunis as Jamie, young NYC based headhunter, and Justin Timberlake as Dylan, online art director from LA, who arrives in New York for an interview with GQ magazine. And true the exploration of benefits is taken to the edge of that well-worn envelope and beyond. “FWB” is randy and profane and funny, even if it’s a runaway cliché. You know the drill: cool guy and hot girl like each other and swear they can be friends even if they have sex. Neither is looking for a commitment. They have tons of chemistry, hangout well, text, and even find themselves in the middle of a Manhattan flash mob, doing what flash mobs do. It’s all kinda cool. But not to forget: benefits signify benefits. No matter the steam on the windows and their amazing mutual attraction. What Jamie and Dylan refuse to acknowledge is what everyone in the audience already knows: they’re in love. Denial (or sustained dissembling when confronted) is not a river in India, but in rom-coms of this ilk it’s a familiar refuge. The tension is nicely developed and drawn out, compounded by Jamie’s conviction that she’s damaged in some vague way and Dylan’s certainty that he’s emotionally unavailable. Both have been told this during past breakups. As romantic comedies go, and there have been a spate of them in the last several years, “FWB” is the exception: it’s really good. The writing is sharp, the pacing is engaging, and both Jamie and Dylan are smart and interesting, especially Jamie. Kunis is wonderful, and if she is an example of the young, metro woman who is confident and fearless, in a funny, quick, and intelligent way, that’s all to the good. Friends With Benefits is light years from It Happened One Night, the 1934 movie with Clark Gable and Claudette Colbert, and way better than anything that has appeared recently, including No Strings Attached a good example. Friends With Benefits. Directed by Will Gluck. Starring Mila Kunis, Justin Timberlake, Patricia Clarkson, Richard Jenkins and Jemma Elfman. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated R

articles.text: Part 31 in a semi-weekly series The important concept of architectural building massing refers to the overall general form, shape, size and orientation of a structure, apart from the more detailed considerations like fenestration, detailing, or textures, all of which enter a little bit later in the design process. Generally, after the decision on architectural style, I would say that overall building massing becomes the most important consideration of any architectural design. It is so important because it forms the “infrastructure” of the whole aesthetic – of all the subsequent design decisions that follow. It is at the apex of the design hierarchy—what is first observable and evident when approaching a building. articles.text: As we enter the fall and winter months, Piedmonters prepare for shorter, darker, and colder days in varying ways. Many of us, including a vast majority of the population of the Northern Hemisphere, bring out cold-weather clothing and spend time preparing for holiday celebrations. For the Southwestern United States, the fall months include long-awaited rain after months-long dry spells. California relies heavily on the precipitation of these wet months to replenish our water supply in the forms of surface water and groundwater. In Northern California, the vast majority of our water originates as snow in the Sierra Nevada region and feeds into a network of surface water sources. In the Bay Area, 60% of the water supply is sourced from the Sierra Nevada snowpack. Of the annual water supplied to the San Francisco Bay Delta, 40% comes from the Sierra snowmelt. Piedmont’s water, supplied by the East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD), comes from the Mokelumne River watershed and is collected in the Pardee Reservoir in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Throughout the winter, the accumulation of water in the snowpack of the Sierra Nevada Mountains is crucial. The snowpack can increase our surface water storage by over 70% by acting like a natural reservoir during the colder months. When water is stored in the mountain snowpack, the delayed rate of release allows this water to slowly melt and accumulate in man-made surface reservoirs as temperatures rise. During our warmer months, precipitation levels fall and water demand is high, but the water stored in the mountain snowpack alleviates seasonal fluctuations in rainfall. However, as global temperatures rise, less water falls as snow in the Sierra Nevada, resulting in decreased snowpack. According to the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Report released in August, the global temperature is expected to reach or exceed 1.5°C of warming above pre-industrial levels in the early 2030s in all emissions scenarios considered. As climate change progresses, Northern Californians will experience high year-to-year variability of precipitation in the form of “booms and busts”, or very wet periods followed by very dry periods. These “whiplash” events will swing our local ecosystem through extreme conditions, with the largest individual storms becoming more intense, accompanied by more frequent extremely dry precipitation periods. One of the results of these changes is greater intensity and persistence of drought, which has ranging impacts here in California including those on agriculture, drinking water, ecosystems, energy, industry, and recreation. Namely, nearly 70% of California’s existing area of wine production may be vulnerable under climate change by mid-century. Meanwhile, decreasing snowpack in the Sierra Nevada’s will threaten the industry and recreation of the area throughout the winter season. Similarly, California’s Forest land, which comprises roughly one-third of the state’s total land area, is threatened by heat and drought, including increased fire frequency and intensity, and new threats such as changing wildlife and insect populations. In Piedmont, residents can not only take overarching measures to combat climate change, such as actions to reduce Greenhouse Gas Emissions, but also to prepare for and increase resilience to drought. Piedmont Connect’s recent event series, “Living with Drought”, highlighted water conserving techniques and presented case-studies on healthy, ecofriendly, water-efficient homes and gardens. One such action, highlighted by the organization’s garden tours, includes adapting gardens and yards to reduce water use and transition away from invasive and water intensive landscaping. Other resources include the Piedmont Climate Challenge and EBMUD. The Piedmont Climate Challenge highlights water-wise changes including mindful lifestyle changes as well as home appliance upgrades to maximize water efficiency. Similarly, the EBMUD website includes a section on Conservation and Rebates, which features the WaterSmart Gardener resource, the WaterSmart Calculator, and information on rebates, programs, and tools that will help residents and businesses increase water efficiency. Annie Wensley is the City of Piedmont’s Civic Spark Fellow. She can be reached at awensley@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: In spite of the threat of rain, 17 fearless members of Walking on Wednesdays group and two K-9 best friends were at the Exedra on Wednesday, October 20 for their weekly stroll through town. Though overcast, not a drop of rain fell on the walkers during their pre-Halloween walk. One of the many things the walkers enjoy about Halloween is the creative decorations on homes. A house at Hampton and Glen Alpine had some especially fun decorations. A home on Lexford Road built in a storyteller architectural style that is unusual, and it seemed appropriate to see it at this time of year. The group had not been on Hampton, Lexford and Huntleigh Roads for a couple of years, so that part of town was selected as the destination. The walkers went up Lincoln Avenue so they could see the decorations on a home in the first block of Crocker which had a large set of skeletons and skulls in the front yard. At King Avenue, a house almost looked like the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch there were so many pumpkins in front. Continuing on Hampton they saw a free library in front of one house. At the corner of Hampton and Glen Alpine they saw two sets of animated characters that included Scooby-Doo and the Flintstones. Crossing La Salle Avenue, they passed through the two large columns marking the entrance to the St. James Woods neighborhood that was developed in the early 20th century. Its streets are still clearly defined by the brown terracotta tiles inlaid in the sidewalks. The walkers went up Lexford to a large, storybook style home built early last century, on a large lot with cobblestones arranged around the front yard. The house’s exterior is made almost entirely of bricks and it has a slate roof. There is even a turret on the middle of the house that gives the look of a castle or fort. A sign at the front door proclaims, “The Roster Crows, but the Hen Delivers.” They also enjoyed the ghosts, skeletons, and other Halloween decorations all around the yard. On the walk they observed lovely gardens with cedar trees, azalea bushes, and fall colors. At the top of street, just before the intersection with La Salle, a large set of skeletons, reclining in garden chairs, watched the walkers go by. None of the walkers had ever visited La Salle Court, a culde-sac, and they couldn’t resist one more new street. Up a fairly steep hill at the top is another large, impressive home with a swimming pool in front. As the group started down the hill, they noticed an abstract statue in a yard that appeared to be a man with broken chains in his outstretched hands. They decided this was Marley’s Ghost, Scrooge’s former business partner in Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol. It was about a 3-mile walk in less than two hours and was time to return to their starting point at the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group, sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation is required at jwilk@ piedmont.ca.gov. At King Avenue, a house almost looked like the Wildwood Dads Club Pumpkin Patch there were so many pumpkins in front. Continuing on Hampton they saw a free library in front of one house. At the corner of Hampton and Glen Alpine they saw two sets of animated characters that included Scooby-Doo and the Flintstones. Crossing La Salle Avenue, they passed through the two large columns marking the entrance to the St. James Woods neighborhood that was developed in the early 20th century. Its streets are still clearly defined by the brown terracotta tiles inlaid in the sidewalks. The walkers went up Lexford to a large, storybook style home built early last century, on a large lot with cobblestones arranged around the front yard. The house’s exterior is made almost entirely of bricks and it has a slate roof. There is even a turret on the middle of the house that gives the look of a castle or fort. A sign at the front door proclaims, “The Roster Crows, but the Hen Delivers.” They also enjoyed the ghosts, skeletons, and other Halloween decorations all around the yard. On the walk they observed lovely gardens with cedar trees, azalea bushes, and fall colors. At the top of street, just before the intersection with La Salle, a large set of skeletons, reclining in garden chairs, watched the walkers go by. None of the walkers had ever visited La Salle Court, a culde-sac, and they couldn’t resist one more new street. Up a fairly steep hill at the top is another large, impressive home with a swimming pool in front. As the group started down the hill, they noticed an abstract statue in a yard that appeared to be a man with broken chains in his outstretched hands. They decided this was Marley’s Ghost, Scrooge’s former business partner in Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol. The suspects are described as follows: One suspect is a black male juvenile, wearing a black hooded sweatshirt, gray sweatpants, Air Jordan 9 black and white shoes, and a dark colored face covering. I suppose it is a combination of style awareness and a common-sense response to surrounding site conditions—all the while providing for the multitude of functional requirements of construction and servicing that the building must accommodate. I think that good architects combine continuing aesthetic consideration, professional experience and past trial and error efforts to arrive at successful architectural massing and composition. In the end, the measure of success is simple: does it work? And does it look good? Next: Architectural Detailing Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com Some think this 9-unit multi-family Piedmont complex might have been designed by the famous modernist architect Irving Gill. It is wonderfully laid out with an inner courtyard with beautiful bay views, and private unit entries. However, I think the building massing is lacking; it would have looked better with another story (and more detail attention to the street side). It is interesting that a bigger building (and additional units) can sometimes improve the building aesthetic and urban design. This beautiful Piedmont house employs a reoccurring massing motif often used by astute architects: an L shaped plan introduces a street facing gable to relieve the long ridge and eave of the main roof. The massing of the deck and porch cover (accentuated by the planting) provides the same relief.
